record.paper_title: Homogenization in mechanics. A survey of solved and open problems
record.original_question: For suspensions of solid particles in a fluid, how can the evolving microstructure be determined well enough to compute the macroscopic flow, including the effects of particle micro-location, applied-force location, and microstructure-dependent coefficients such as homogenized viscosity?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a suspension consisting of a large number of small rigid solid particles immersed in a viscous Newtonian fluid that occupies a bounded macroscopic domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ ($d=2,3$). At time $t=0$, the particles are distributed in $\Omega$ with a prescribed (possibly random) microstructure characterized by a small parameter $\varepsilon>0$ measuring the typical inter-particle distance. The fluid satisfies the (Navier–)Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions on each particle, the particles move and rotate rigidly under hydrodynamic and applied body forces, and an external force field $f(x,t)$ acts on the suspension.

Develop a quantitative theory describing the time evolution of the microstructure, together with a closed effective (homogenized) system for the macroscopic velocity and pressure on $\Omega$, with the following properties:

1. The effective system must involve an effective viscosity tensor (and possibly additional effective constitutive coefficients) that depend on the instantaneous microstructure, including local particle volume fraction and statistical descriptors of particle arrangement.

2. The theory must track the sensitivity of the effective behavior to the precise micro-location of the particles and to the spatial location of applied forces, in the sense that it explains and quantifies how perturbations of these data affect both the evolved microstructure and the homogenized coefficients.

3. The effective microstructure-evolution law and the effective fluid equations must be consistent with the underlying particle–fluid system in the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$, in a rigorous sense (e.g. convergence of solutions and of macroscopic quantities such as stress and dissipation).

Provide such a closed effective model, prove its well-posedness, and establish its rigorous derivation from the microscopic particle–fluid system, or otherwise determine the obstructions to doing so.
artifact.status_search_result: The literature shows active mathematical work on homogenization for rigid suspensions and effective viscosity (e.g., Einstein-type formulas, rigorous derivations for dilute and moderately dense regimes), but determining the evolving microstructure together with location-dependent homogenized coefficients for the macroscopic flow is still considered an open challenge. Existing results address either fixed microstructures, dilute limits, or formal evolution laws, without a complete rigorous closure.

status_evidence.title: Homogenization for Rigid Suspensions with Random Velocity-Dependent Interfacial Forces
status_evidence.snippet: Rigorous homogenization for rigid suspensions in Stokes flow with random interfacial forces, yielding effective equations under structural assumptions.
status_evidence.claim: Rigorous homogenization results exist for special suspension regimes, but not for general evolving microstructures.

status_evidence.title: Homogenisation in domains with evolving microstructure
status_evidence.snippet: General approach to homogenization in evolving microstructures via transformation to a fixed periodic reference domain.
status_evidence.claim: Frameworks for evolving microstructure homogenization exist but rely on transformations and do not give a complete closure for suspensions.

status_evidence.title: Macroscopic modeling of the evolution of fiber orientation during flow
status_evidence.snippet: Microstructural evolution laws (orientation tensors) are coupled with homogenization models to characterize time-dependent suspension response, with closure approximations.
status_evidence.claim: Engineering models couple microstructure evolution with homogenization but require closure assumptions, indicating the mathematical problem is still open.
